TITLE: Photosynthesis: Light into Sugar

INTRO: You already know plants need light. Here you will pin down the exact inputs, the energy source, the pigment that captures it, and the by-product. These practice items just show what stuck, so keep them low-stakes. Warm-up: name one gas you breathe out, and one green part of a plant.

SECTION 1 - The reaction: inputs and outputs
Rule: photosynthesis builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water. The arrow chain is carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen. Oxygen leaves as a by-product; glucose is the product the plant keeps.
EXAMPLE: A basketball box score lists points first and assists second: glucose is the headline product, oxygen the by-product line. Try it: Name the two inputs. Answer: carbon dioxide and water.

SECTION 2 - Capturing the energy
Rule: the reaction needs light energy, which comes from the sun. Chlorophyll, the green pigment inside chloroplasts, absorbs that light. Without chlorophyll, the main light-capture step fails.
EXAMPLE: A video game power-up needs your character to make contact; chlorophyll is the leaf's contact point for light. Try it: What absorbs the light? Answer: chlorophyll in the chloroplasts.

SECTION 3 - Where it happens
Rule: photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves. A leaf is broad and flat, so it catches light and lets carbon dioxide in. The same leaf holds the chloroplasts where chlorophyll sits.
EXAMPLE: In a comic panel you would draw arrows into the leaf for carbon dioxide and water, sunlight hitting the chlorophyll, and arrows out for glucose and oxygen. Try it: In which organ does most photosynthesis happen? Answer: the leaves.

WORKED EXAMPLE: You are drawing a comic panel of a leaf making sugar. Before reading the steps, sketch it: label two inputs, the energy source, the pigment, and two outputs.
  1. Inputs: carbon dioxide enters the leaf from the air, and water arrives from the soil through the roots.
  2. Energy: draw sunlight hitting the leaf, because the reaction uses light energy from the sun.
  3. Capture: label chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts, because that pigment absorbs the light.
  4. Outputs: draw glucose staying in the plant and oxygen leaving as a by-product.
  5. Location: set the whole panel in a leaf, because photosynthesis happens mainly there.
  ANSWER: Panel labels: carbon dioxide and water in; sunlight; chlorophyll in chloroplasts; glucose and oxygen out; all inside a leaf.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: Plants get their food from the soil, so photosynthesis takes in soil and releases carbon dioxide. Why: soil supplies water and minerals, not glucose; the gas released is oxygen, a by-product. Right: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen, with chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbing the light.

SUMMARY: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen, with chlorophyll in leaf chloroplasts absorbing the light. Oxygen is the by-product; leaves are the main site.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. Which statement matches photosynthesis? [choices: Plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide to make glucose. | Plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. | Plants absorb sugar from soil and store it in leaves. | Plants make oxygen from glucose and water in chloroplasts.] -> Plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
2. A leaf has water and carbon dioxide but is kept in complete darkness. Which step of the chain fails, and what happens to the outputs? [typed answer] -> The light-capture step fails because chlorophyll has no light to absorb, so glucose and oxygen are not produced.
texts.mirror:
TITLE: Photosynthesis: How a Leaf Makes Its Own Food

INTRO: A plant cannot walk to a shop, so it makes its own food inside itself. This lesson shows you what goes in, what gets made, and what is left over. You will follow every step on one leaf, then try it yourself.

SECTION 1 - The rule: carbon dioxide plus water, using light, makes glucose
Photosynthesis is the way a plant makes its own food. A plant takes in carbon dioxide, a gas that is in the air all around it. It also takes in water, which its roots pull up from the soil. Then it uses light energy, meaning power that travels as light from the sun, to join those two things into glucose, a sugar that is the plant's food. So the rule is: carbon dioxide plus water, using light energy, makes glucose.
EXAMPLE: Think of a video game where you buy a sword. You need two coins, and you need a power-up before the shop will let you buy. Carbon dioxide and water are the two coins. Light energy is the power-up. Glucose is the sword the plant ends up holding.

SECTION 2 - Chlorophyll catches the light
The light does not get used on its own; something in the leaf has to catch it. Inside leaf cells are tiny packets called chloroplasts. Each chloroplast is packed with chlorophyll, a green substance that absorbs light. To absorb means to soak up and hold. Chlorophyll looks green because it soaks up the other colours of light and reflects green back to your eye.
EXAMPLE: Say you are drawing comics and you colour a leaf with a green pencil. The green pencil looks green to your reader for the same reason chlorophyll does: it sends green light back and holds the rest. That is how you know where the light-catching stuff in a leaf is, because the green marks the chlorophyll.

SECTION 3 - Oxygen is left over, and it happens mainly in the leaves
When carbon dioxide and water are joined into glucose, oxygen is left over. Oxygen is released as a by-product, meaning something made along the way that the plant does not need. The plant lets the oxygen out through the same small holes it took carbon dioxide in through. Nearly all of photosynthesis happens in the leaves, because that is where the chloroplasts are. A little can also happen in green stems, which is why we say mainly in the leaves.
EXAMPLE: In a basketball game, the team scores and the arena throws out free T-shirts. The shirts are not the point of the game; they just fly out anyway. Oxygen is like those shirts: glucose is the point, and oxygen leaves as a by-product.

Try it: A green stem can photosynthesise a little. Why do we still say photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves? Answer: Leaves hold nearly all the chloroplasts, so they are where nearly all the light is absorbed.

WORKED EXAMPLE: You are drawing a comic that shows a leaf as a tiny factory. Your reader asks three things: what goes in, what gets made, and what comes out. Trace it with every step shown.
  1. Step 1. Start outside the leaf. Sunlight lands on the leaf. This is the light energy that will be used.
  2. Step 2. Inside the leaf are cells, and inside the cells are chloroplasts. The chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs the light, so the light energy is now caught and held.
  3. Step 3. At the same time, carbon dioxide from the air goes into the leaf through small holes. That is coin one.
  4. Step 4. Water travels up from the roots and reaches the leaf. That is coin two.
  5. Step 5. The caught light energy is used to join the carbon dioxide and the water into glucose. Glucose is the sugar the plant uses as food, so the plant has now made its own food.
  6. Step 6. Oxygen is left over from that joining. The plant does not need it, so it leaves the leaf through the small holes as a by-product.
  7. Step 7. Check the picture: inputs are carbon dioxide and water, the power is light energy caught by chlorophyll in chloroplasts, the product is glucose, and the by-product is oxygen. All of this happens mainly in the leaves.
  ANSWER: Carbon dioxide and water go in. Light energy from the sun is absorbed by chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts. Glucose is made as the plant's food. Oxygen leaves as a by-product. This happens mainly in the leaves.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: "Plants get their food from the soil." Why: the soil supplies water and minerals, not sugar, so the food step breaks here; a plant makes its own glucose in its leaves. Right: carbon dioxide plus water, using light energy, makes glucose.
Wrong: "Photosynthesis happens mainly in the roots." Why: roots sit in the dark and hold no chlorophyll, so no light is absorbed there and the light-catching step breaks. Right: photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, where chloroplasts full of chlorophyll absorb the light.
Wrong: "Plants take in oxygen to make their food, and oxygen is what plants eat." Why: oxygen is not an input and not the food; it is left over after glucose is made, so this swaps the by-product for the product. Right: carbon dioxide and water go in, glucose is made, and oxygen is released as a by-product.

SUMMARY: Photosynthesis is how a plant feeds itself: carbon dioxide and water, using light energy from the sun, are joined into glucose. Chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts of leaves absorbs that light. Oxygen is released as a by-product, and the whole thing happens mainly in the leaves.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. Hint: think of the gas animals breathe out. Which gas does a plant take in from the air to make glucose? [choices: Oxygen | Carbon dioxide | Nitrogen | Water vapour] -> Carbon dioxide
2. Hint: it is the green stuff, and it sits inside the tiny packets in leaf cells. What is the name of the green substance that absorbs light? [typed answer] -> Chlorophyll
3. Hint: check the inputs and check where the chloroplasts are. A learner writes: "A plant's food comes from the soil, and photosynthesis happens mainly in the roots." Which line fixes both mistakes? [choices: Food is water from the soil; photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves. | Food is glucose made in the leaves; photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves. | Food is glucose made in the roots; photosynthesis happens mainly in the roots. | Food is oxygen; photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves.] -> Food is glucose made in the leaves; photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves.
